lesson_title: Zero Is the Number That Confesses
hook_text: Two takings multiplied together make zero. You already know someone's secret.
clip_script: Two classmates run a koeksister table at market day. At closing, you're told one thing: their two takings, multiplied together, come to zero. You instantly know something solid — at least one of them sold absolutely nothing. Multiplication has no other way to make zero. Now change the story: the takings multiply to six hundred rand. What do you know about the first classmate? Nothing. Six hundred could be six hundred times one, thirty times twenty, ten times sixty. Six hundred keeps secrets. Zero confesses. That is the entire reason your quadratic must equal zero before you factorise. See x plus one, times x minus four, equals six? You may NOT say x plus one is six — six forces nothing. Expand, move the six across: x squared minus three x minus ten equals zero. Factorise: x minus five, times x plus two. NOW there's a zero on the right, so one bracket must be empty. x is five, or x is minus two. One more trap: never divide an equation by x. x squared equals seven x? Divide by x and the answer zero vanishes forever. Factor the x out instead — x times x minus seven equals zero — and zero confesses all by itself.
visual_style: Split-screen market stall: two jars of coins with a multiplication sign between them, one jar emptying to zero with a spotlight snapping onto it; then handwritten algebra unrolling on brown paper, brackets snapping shut like till drawers.
mood: Playful detective energy — a confession being extracted.
pacing: Quick setup, a freeze on the zero reveal, brisk through the algebra.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make every quadratic confess.
